wrong.They face the same: B has a year of trapped buyers above it. A has almost none from the past year.

questions.q: A stock's high is $80. It now trades at $68. How far down from its high is it, in percent?
questions.why: 15%. Subtract the price from the high, divide by the high, and write it as a percent.
questions.lesson_line: We read a chart in percents: down from highs, extended from the averages. Percents compare across stocks.

questions.q: On a daily chart, what makes a gap down?
choices: Today's high is below yesterday's low
Today's low is above yesterday's high
Today's range is smaller than usual
questions.answer: Today's high is below yesterday's low
questions.why: Today's high is below yesterday's low. That leaves an empty space on the chart where no trading took place.
questions.lesson_line: A gap down leaves a hole above the price. Gaps often mark support or resistance zones.

wrong.Today closes below yesterday's close: That's just a down day. On a chart, a gap needs empty space between the two days' ranges.
wrong.Today's range is smaller than usual: That's a narrow day. A gap is about the space between days, not the size of one.

questions.q: Any gap on a chart is sure to get filled sooner or later.
questions.why: False. Common gaps usually fill fast, but breakaway gaps often don't. In bull markets, Bulkowski found only 1% of upward breakaway gaps closed within a week.
questions.lesson_line: Don't sit out a strong breakaway gap waiting for a fill. It may never come.

questions.q: Which word is this: a gap late in a long move, on heavy volume, that closes within days as the trend ends.
questions.why: Exhaustion gap. It comes at the end of a trend on high volume, and it usually closes within a week as price reverses.
questions.lesson_line: A huge gap after a long run can be the last gasp. Watch whether it closes.

wrong.Breakaway gap: A breakaway gap starts a trend as price leaves a range, and it rarely closes fast.
wrong.Runaway gap: A runaway gap comes mid-trend, and price keeps making new highs without closing it.
wrong.Common gap: Common gaps form inside quiet ranges, not at the end of a long trend.

questions.story: A stock broke out of a base weeks ago and has climbed almost straight up. Today it gaps up again on heavy volume. For weeks after, it keeps making new highs and never comes back to the gap.
questions.q: Which gap type fits best?
questions.why: Runaway gap. It came in the middle of a straight-line advance, and price kept making new highs without closing it. It's also called a measuring or continuation gap.
questions.lesson_line: A gap mid-trend that never fills is strength. Don't wait for it to close before you trust the trend.

wrong.Exhaustion gap: An exhaustion gap is usually not followed by new highs and tends to close fast. This one did the opposite.
wrong.Breakaway gap: A breakaway gap starts the move as price leaves a base. This one came weeks into the run.
wrong.Common gap: Common gaps form in quiet, trendless stretches and close within days.

questions.story: A stock ran from $10 to $80 in two years. On your chart, the move from $10 to $20 looks the same size as $70 to $80.
questions.q: Which price scale would show $10 to $20 as the bigger move?
questions.why: Log scale. $10 to $20 is a 100% gain, and $70 to $80 is a much smaller one. A log scale spaces moves by percent, so the bigger percent looks bigger.
questions.lesson_line: On long charts and big movers, use log scale. Percent is what your account feels.

wrong.Arithmetic scale: That's the scale you're on. It spaces every dollar the same, so $70 to $80 looks as big as $10 to $20.
wrong.A shorter timeframe: Zooming in changes the window, not how price is spaced. The scale is the fix.

questions.q: Today's high is $52.40 and today's low is $50.10. What is the day's range in dollars?
questions.why: $2.30. The range is the high minus the low for the period.
questions.lesson_line: Range is how far a stock travels in a session. Know it before you set a stop.

questions.q: A stock rallies from $40 to $60, then pulls back to $50. What percent of the rally has it given back?
questions.why: 50%. Divide the drop from the top by the size of the rally. Dow Theory's Hamilton called half the typical retracement, inside a one-third to two-thirds range.
questions.lesson_line: Measure a pullback as a share of the rally. Past two-thirds, ChartSchool says a reversal is more likely.

questions.q: The S&P 500 peaks at 5,000 and falls to 4,400. How far is it down from the peak, in percent?
questions.why: 12%. That's past the 10% line most people use for a correction, and short of the 20% that usually marks a bear market.
questions.lesson_line: A 10% drop from the peak is the usual line for a correction; 20% for a bear market.

questions.q: Generally, a bear market means a broad market index has fallen 20% or more over at least two months.
questions.why: True. That's the SEC's Investor.gov definition, given as a general rule, not a law.
questions.lesson_line: A 20% drop from the peak in a broad index is the usual line for a bear market.

questions.q: Which word is this: you act on a buy signal, and the price reverses against you within days.
questions.why: Whipsaw. The signal flipped in a short time. Volatile markets and sensitive indicators can cause them.
questions.lesson_line: Whipsaws are a cost of trading signals. A stop keeps each one small.

wrong.Accumulation: Accumulation is big buyers quietly building positions in a range.
wrong.Breakaway gap: A breakaway gap is a gap that starts a new move.
wrong.Golden cross: A golden cross is a shorter moving average crossing above a longer one.

questions.q: How do you draw an uptrend line?
questions.why: Connect the rising lows. Two lows draw the line, and a third touch confirms it.
questions.lesson_line: Uptrend lines go under the lows. The more clean touches, the more the line matters.

wrong.Connect the rising highs: In an uptrend, a line over the rally peaks is the channel line, the upper edge.
wrong.Connect the closing prices: That's a line chart, not a trendline.

questions.q: When price breaks below an uptrend line, the uptrend has reversed.
questions.why: False. A trendline break is a warning, not a verdict. ChartSchool says a change in trend may be coming, and to confirm it with support levels and the peaks and troughs. Investopedia says only that a break could mean a reversal.
questions.lesson_line: A broken trendline says pay attention. A lower low says the uptrend is done.

questions.q: In its first few days, a reversal can look exactly like an ordinary pullback.
questions.why: True. Investopedia puts it plainly: for a few critical sessions they look identical. Dow Theory adds that people often mistake a counter-move for a new trend.
questions.lesson_line: You won't know at the start. That's why the stop goes in before you find out.

questions.q: What is a pullback?
choices: A short dip inside an uptrend
A change from uptrend to downtrend
A break above the last high
questions.answer: A short dip inside an uptrend
questions.why: A short dip inside an uptrend. Price eases back, often toward support or a moving average, then the uptrend resumes. If it doesn't, it was a reversal.
questions.lesson_line: Pullbacks in strong uptrends are one of the two classic places to buy. A new high is the other.

wrong.A change from uptrend to downtrend: That's a reversal. A pullback is temporary, and the uptrend carries on.
wrong.A break above the last high: That's a breakout, price clearing a level that held it. A pullback is a dip, not a push higher.

conflicts: Pullback vs throwback: Bulkowski (glossary, throwbacks page) and Fidelity's Kirkpatrick slides call a return to the breakout price after an UPWARD breakout a 'throwback' and keep 'pullback' for the return after a DOWNWARD breakout. Investopedia, ChartSchool's moving-average page and everyday usage call any short dip inside an uptrend a pullback. The unit uses the everyday meaning for pullback (q63, q39) and teaches throwback only in Bulkowski's sense (q17); no question asks which side of a breakout a 'pullback' follows.

Exhaustion gap: ChartSchool (glossary G and the gaps article) and Bulkowski agree it is a gap IN the direction of a long move, near its end, closed soon. Investopedia's gap page describes it as 'a break lower in prices (usually on a daily chart) that occurs after a rapid rise'. q52 keys the ChartSchool/Bulkowski version; Investopedia's wording is not used.

What counts as a gap: ChartSchool and Bulkowski define it by the whole range (today's high below yesterday's low for a down gap). Investopedia also counts a 'partial gap' (an open beyond the prior close but inside the prior range) and defines a 'full gap' by the open. q50 uses the full-range definition from the two that agree.

Correction: ChartSchool's glossary (C) defines a correction technically, as a decline that retraces 1/3 to 2/3 of an advance. Schwab and Investopedia use the index convention: a decline of more than 10% from a peak (Schwab adds 'but less than 20%'; Investopedia gives no upper bound). q57 asks only for the computed percent and words the 10% line as the convention 'most people use'.

Leader: ChartSchool's glossary defines a leader as an industry or company outperforming the market, and an Interactive Brokers webinar by Dan Russo, CMT, says relative strength shows whether a stock 'is leading or lagging its peers'. Investopedia's 'Market Leader' page is the business meaning (largest market share). Nasdaq's leaders-vs-laggards articles and investors.com refused both clients, and Investopedia's CAN SLIM page (read from the Internet Archive) muddles O'Neil's L ('Laggard stocks are preferred ... Use the relative strength index'), so neither was used. q33 keys the chart meaning and names the business meaning in the reveal.

Base: ChartSchool's 'Basing' is a flat trading range after a decline; growth-stock usage (O'Neil, IBD) also calls a consolidation after an advance a base; Bulkowski's flat base is a flat price area touched repeatedly over weeks or months. q42 keys only the shared part: a sideways range lasting weeks or more, with no clear trend. Base anatomy is V.04's job.

Coil: only ChartSchool (symmetrical triangle page) names the narrowing pattern a 'coil'; I found no second Tier 2 publisher using the word. q46's key does not rest on the word: it rests on the point two publishers agree on, that a narrowing range gives no clue to direction (ChartSchool triangle and squeeze pages; Investopedia sideways market: the old trend may continue or a new one start).

52-week high: Investopedia's 52-week page says the figure is 'based on the security's daily closing price'; ChartSchool and Investopedia's breakout page speak of the highest price. Data vendors differ. q47's answer ('its highest price in the past year') holds either way, and no question asks close vs intraday.

Breakout: Investopedia, ChartSchool and Bulkowski count a break below support as a (downside) breakout; most traders call it a breakdown, as Investopedia itself notes ('a downside breakout, often called a breakdown'). q12 keys 'a move through resistance or support' so neither reading is marked wrong; q13 keys breakdown, and its word bank leaves 'breakout' out so the downside reading cannot make a second right answer.

Extended: ChartSchool's glossary measures it from the pivot (buy point); IBD's well-known 5% buy-zone rule was not used because investors.com refuses this tool's crawler. Our own usage (owner: '% extended from MAs') measures it in percent above the moving averages. q25 and q26 are asked as ours (house: true) with ChartSchool's distance-from-moving-average method as the Tier 2 backing.

RSI levels: ChartSchool notes some traders move the levels to 80/20 and short-term traders use other settings. q28 asks only for the traditional level (Wilder's 70/30, stated by ChartSchool, Investopedia and Fidelity).

Relative strength vs RSI: Investopedia's 'Relative Strength' page discusses RSI as a companion tool in the same article, which blurs the two. ChartSchool's Price Relative page (a ratio against a benchmark) and both RSI pages (average gain vs average loss of the stock itself) keep them apart; q31 and q32 follow those.

Existing bank skill vocab.chart (29 chart-picture items: trending, downtrend, coiled, higher lows, inside day, gapping, heavy volume, near its highs, at the 20 EMA, pullback) is not repeated: this unit asks words in text form, and where it reuses a word (pullback, heavy volume, coiled, uptrend) it asks a different thing about it. Inside day is left to V.03 (candle words).

Trendline breaks: Murphy's 10 laws on ChartSchool (f233) say a break 'usually signals a change in trend'; ChartSchool's trend lines page says a break is 'merely a warning that a change in trend may be imminent', and Investopedia that it 'could indicate' a reversal. q61's statement is absolute ('the uptrend has reversed'), which is false under all three, so its key stands; f233 is kept here and not cited in q61, so the reveal never seems to argue with its own key. ChartSchool's glossary T says the same as Murphy ('The breaking of a trend line usually signals a trend reversal'); 'usually signals' is still not 'has reversed', and ChartSchool's trend lines page shows a break that did not reverse the trend.
